##### **1.8 Relative Motion, Collisions, and Pursuit Problems**

In multi-body kinematics, describing motion in an alternative reference frame simplifies the equations of motion by eliminating common drift or isolating mutual approach rates. For two material points with position vectors $\vec{r}_1(t)$ and $\vec{r}_2(t)$ in an inertial frame, the **relative position** of point 1 with respect to point 2 is $\vec{r}_{12} = \vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2$, and the **relative velocity** is $\vec{v}_{12} = \frac{d\vec{r}_{12}}{dt} = \vec{v}_1 - \vec{v}_2$.

###### **1.8.1 Vector Condition for Particle Interception**

Two particles moving with constant velocities $\vec{v}_1$ and $\vec{v}_2$ from initial positions $\vec{r}_1$ and $\vec{r}_2$ collide at a common location $\vec{r}_3$ at time $t > 0$ if and only if their trajectories intersect simultaneously:

$$\vec{r}_3 = \vec{r}_1 + \vec{v}_1 t = \vec{r}_2 + \vec{v}_2 t.$$

Rearranging terms groups initial spatial separation and relative velocity:

$$\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2 = (\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1)t. \tag{1}$$

Taking the Euclidean norm of both sides isolates the scalar travel time to interception:

$$t = \frac{|\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2|}{|\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1|}. \tag{2}$$

Substituting $(2)$ into $(1)$ eliminates $t$, yielding the collinearity criterion for collision:

$$\frac{\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2}{|\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2|} = \frac{\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1}{|\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1|}.$$

A collision occurs if and only if the unit vector along the initial separation line is strictly identical to the unit vector along the relative velocity $\vec{v}_{21} = \vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1$. In the rest frame of particle 2, particle 1 moves directly along the line of sight toward the origin.

###### **1.8.2 Invariant Interaction Time**

When a problem contains oscillatory or alternating trajectories between converging boundaries, solving the boundary motion directly determines the total duration, bypassing recursive infinite series. 

Consider two trains moving along a single track directly toward each other from an initial separation $D = 60\text{ km}$, each at constant speed $V_b = 30\text{ km/h}$. A bird flies back and forth between them at constant speed $V_w = 60\text{ km/h}$ until the trains collide. In the ground frame, the mutual approach speed of the two trains is $2V_b$, yielding the collision time:

$$t = \frac{D}{2V_b} = \frac{60\text{ km}}{2 \times 30\text{ km/h}} = 1\text{ h}.$$

Because the bird travels continuously at constant speed $V_w$ over this exact duration, its total traversed distance $S$ depends only on the invariant time $t$:

$$S = V_w t = 60\text{ km/h} \times 1\text{ h} = 60\text{ km}.$$

###### **1.8.3 Bounded One-Dimensional Pursuit**

In rectilinear pursuit, a pursuer with speed $v_C$ chases a target with speed $v_A < v_C$ moving along the same line with an initial spatial lead $d_0$. Setting coordinates $x_C(t) = v_C t$ and $x_A(t) = d_0 + v_A t$ gives the capture time:

$$t_{\text{catch}} = \frac{d_0}{v_C - v_A}.$$

When the pursuer can sustain its maximum speed only over a finite duration $t_{\max}$, capture requires $t_{\text{catch}} \le t_{\max}$. The maximum initial head start permissible for capture is:

$$d_{\max} = (v_C - v_A) t_{\max}.$$

* **Worked illustration:** A cheetah runs at $v_C = 101\text{ km/h} = \frac{101}{3.6}\text{ m/s} \approx 28.06\text{ m/s}$ with an endurance limit $t_{\max} = 20\text{ s}$. An antelope runs at $v_A = 88\text{ km/h} = \frac{88}{3.6}\text{ m/s} \approx 24.44\text{ m/s}$. The relative speed is:
  $$\Delta v = v_C - v_A = \frac{13}{3.6}\text{ m/s} \approx 3.61\text{ m/s}.$$
  With an initial lead $d_0 = 40\text{ m}$, the time required is $t_{\text{catch}} = \frac{40}{3.61} \approx 11.08\text{ s} \le 20\text{ s}$, covering a distance $x_C = 28.06 \times 11.08 \approx 311\text{ m}$. The maximum catchable head start over $20\text{ s}$ is $d_{\max} = 3.61\text{ m/s} \times 20\text{ s} \approx 72.2\text{ m}$.

###### **1.8.4 Symmetrical Multi-Agent Pursuit**

In symmetrical pursuit geometries, multiple particles simultaneously adjust their heading angles toward their respective targets. Consider three identical particles placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of initial side length $a$, each moving with constant speed $v$ and heading continually toward the next in cyclic order.

```{tikz}
#| label: fig-pursuit-triangle
#| fig-cap: "Velocity decomposition along the line connecting mutually pursuing particles."
#| echo: false
#| lang: tex
#| fig-height: 3.2
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.1, every node/.style={font=\small}]
  \coordinate (A) at (0, 0);
  \coordinate (B) at (4, 0);
  \coordinate (C) at (2, 3.464);
  
  \draw[dashed, thick, color=gray!60] (A) -- (B) -- (C) -- cycle;
  
  \filldraw[black] (A) circle (2pt) node[below left] {$1$};
  \filldraw[black] (B) circle (2pt) node[below right] {$2$};
  \filldraw[black] (C) circle (2pt) node[above] {$3$};
  
  % Velocity vectors
  \draw[->, >=stealth, very thick, red!80!black] (A) -- (1.5, 0) node[midway, below] {$\vec{v}_1$};
  \draw[->, >=stealth, very thick, red!80!black] (B) -- (3.0, 1.732) node[midway, right] {$\vec{v}_2$};
  \draw[->, >=stealth, very thick, red!80!black] (C) -- (1.0, 1.732) node[midway, left] {$\vec{v}_3$};
  
  % Decomposition of v2 at vertex 2 along line AB
  \draw[->, >=stealth, thick, blue!70!black] (B) -- (3.25, 0) node[below] {$\vec{v}_{2,\parallel}$};
  \draw[->, >=stealth, thick, blue!70!black] (B) -- (4.0, 1.3) node[right] {$\vec{v}_{2,\perp}$};
  \draw[dotted, thick, gray] (3.25, 0) -- (3.25, 1.3) -- (3.0, 1.732);
  
  \draw (3.5, 0) arc (180:120:0.5);
  \node at (3.4, 0.3) {$\frac{\pi}{3}$};
  
  \node at (2, -0.35) {$l(t)$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

By three-fold rotational symmetry, the particles remain at the vertices of a contracting, rotating equilateral triangle at all times $t$, meeting at the triangle centroid. The instantaneous separation $l(t)$ between particle 1 and particle 2 decreases due to two contributions along their line of separation:
1. Particle 1 moves directly toward particle 2 with velocity component $v$.
2. Particle 2 heads toward particle 3 at an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$ radians ($60^\circ$) to the line connecting particle 1 and 2. Its velocity projected onto the segment connecting 1 and 2 points away from particle 1 with magnitude $v \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}v$.

The approach rate $-\frac{dl}{dt}$ is the difference in longitudinal velocity components:

$$-\frac{dl}{dt} = v - \left(-v \cos\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = v + \frac{1}{2}v = \frac{3}{2}v.$$

Because $v$ is constant, the rate of contraction is constant. Integrating from $l(0) = a$ to $l(t) = 0$:

$$-\int_a^0 dl = \frac{3}{2}v \int_0^t dt' \implies a = \frac{3}{2}vt \implies t = \frac{2a}{3v}.$$

The total distance traveled by each particle along its spiral trajectory is $S = vt = \frac{2}{3}a$.

###### **1.8.5 Motion in Accelerating Reference Frames**

In an accelerating reference frame with translational acceleration $\vec{a}_0(t)$ relative to an inertial shaft, any freely falling body experiencing gravitational acceleration $\vec{g}$ exhibits an apparent acceleration:

$$\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{g} - \vec{a}_0.$$

Consider an elevator cabin ascending with uniform vertical acceleration $a_e$ along a vertical $y$-axis ($+y$ upward). At time $t_0 = 2.0\text{ s}$ after starting from rest, a bolt detaches from the ceiling at height $h = 2.7\text{ m}$ above the floor. At detachment, the cabin and the bolt possess upward velocity $v_0 = a_e t_0 = (1.2\text{ m/s}^2)(2.0\text{ s}) = 2.4\text{ m/s}$.

* **Cabin frame analysis:** The cabin accelerates upward at $\vec{a}_0 = a_e \hat{\jmath}$, while gravity acts downward as $\vec{g} = -g \hat{\jmath}$. Relative to the cabin, the downward acceleration of the bolt is:
  $$a_{\text{rel}} = g + a_e = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 + 1.2\text{ m/s}^2 = 11.0\text{ m/s}^2.$$
  Since the bolt is released from rest relative to the cabin ($v_{\text{rel},0} = 0$), the fall time through height $h$ satisfies:
  $$h = \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{rel}} t_{\text{fall}}^2 \implies t_{\text{fall}} = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g + a_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 2.7\text{ m}}{11.0\text{ m/s}^2}} \approx 0.70\text{ s}.$$

* **Shaft frame verification:** In the stationary elevator shaft frame, taking the floor position at $t_0$ as $y = 0$, the floor coordinate evolves as:
  $$y_{\text{floor}}(t) = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}a_e t^2.$$
  The bolt starts at $y_{\text{bolt}}(0) = h$ with initial velocity $v_0$ and accelerates under gravity alone:
  $$y_{\text{bolt}}(t) = h + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}g t^2.$$
  Equating $y_{\text{bolt}}(t) = y_{\text{floor}}(t)$ gives:
  $$h + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}g t^2 = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}a_e t^2 \implies h = \frac{1}{2}(g + a_e)t^2,$$
  which recovers identical fall time $t_{\text{fall}} \approx 0.70\text{ s}$.
  
  During this interval, the displacement of the bolt relative to the fixed shaft is:
  $$\Delta y_{\text{bolt}} = v_0 t_{\text{fall}} - \frac{1}{2}g t_{\text{fall}}^2 = (2.4\text{ m/s})(0.70\text{ s}) - \frac{1}{2}(9.8\text{ m/s}^2)(0.70\text{ s})^2 \approx 1.68 - 2.40 = -0.72\text{ m}.$$
  The bolt rises to an apex before dropping below its detachment coordinate, traveling an upward distance $s_{\text{up}} = \frac{v_0^2}{2g} = \frac{2.4^2}{2 \times 9.8} \approx 0.29\text{ m}$ followed by a downward fall of $s_{\text{down}} = 0.29 + 0.72 = 1.01\text{ m}$, giving a total path length of $s = 1.30\text{ m}$ in the shaft frame.
